questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go somewhere in the US where I could potentially see myself live in the future. This included appealing culture, good weather and a not too small city. Also, the fact that UT Austin is well-ranked university in the world on many measures.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. UT does a great job arranging events in the first few weeks and sending out information and hosting live webinars in advance.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I attended many intro events called "orientations".

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy if you are looking to find something similar to a Danish "kollegie". I would highly recommend the concept of "co-ops" where you live together with other people. Specifically, I lived in a place called "Halstead" in west campus which is run by the organization "College Houses". Based on visiting some other places and meeting people from there, Halstead might be the best combination of relative price level, cleanliness, noise-level, and closeness to campus. Be aware that some co-ops turn into loud party houses with hundreds of people on the weekends (for instance, "21st" and "Pearl").

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Off-campus can mean many things. It includes "west campus" which is the area right next to the UT campus itself, and this varies a lot in price. This is basically filled with only UT students, which gives such a great vibe, very different to anything in Copenhagen, especially in the night. Seems pretty safe and you often see UT police cars patrol around the streets.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration platform opens up first at a certain date and time "normal" full-degree students. Then, after they have registered for courses, it opens up for international students at a later point. Then courses are filled up on a first-come-first-served basis. It is fairly simple, but be sure to have done your research in advance so that you are ready to find and type in your preferred course titles and code numbers in a split second when the registration opens. Otherwise all spots on some popular courses might get taken in quickly. 

Importantly, there is a so-called "add-n-drop" period in the first week or two of the semester where students can drop out of their registered courses and register for new ones if vacant spot. Thus, there is a waitlist function you can use, in case someone drops a course that you want.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Live Zoom meeting running in the meantime with advisors for pop-in questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Managed to register for all my three required courses in the end, one or two by waitlist, and got two additional elective courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do your research, be ready on time when registration opens, have backups ready, and use the waitlist function in case your preferred courses are filled up.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: One introductory "lower division" course and four "upper division" courses. Lower division more lecture hall style with many people and less interaction with professor (like BA psychology at KU). Upper division much smaller classes with more interaction.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Similarly informal, but with more respectfulness towards professors. Also much more interaction and the opportunity to make a personal impression and get a relation to your professor.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.answer: Not many apart from an occasional small fee for stuff like learning software or an ID card at UT.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Depending on where you buy your household items; "Target" at campus pretty expensive, Walmart much cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Hundreds of clubs and organizations to join.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Many kinds of sports (volleyball, ultimate, swimming, soccer, football, basketball etc) and political and social activities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to as many intro events as possible in the beginning. Specifically the walking tour: excellent way to meet new friends and get better at finding your way around campus. I met one friend who made the rest of my semester so much better.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: For Austin: Zilker Park, Barton Springs, downtown, the Texas Capitol, the UT museums. For weekends: find a car and go to Fort Worth, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio or Enchanted Rock. For fall or winter break: go to Big Bend National Park or other states.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be open, say hi, and ask questions about American/Texan/Austin culture.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None really.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The whole UT culture. It is just something completely different from anything you find back in Denmark or maybe even Europe. Great in so many ways, making you feel like a part of a distinct community with its history, traditions, events and everything in a matter of weeks (much more than KU does).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Courses: Do your research and get the courses you need/want.

Housing: Find a place where you are not isolated, but live with a mix of Americans and international students (like a co-op).

Balance: Find your own balance of studying vs socializing vs exploring. Some people are there only to have fun and party every weekend, some people are there to ace their grades for career purposes, and some people are everywhere in between.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: A note on the observation that many Danish people seem to have some preconceived negative beliefs about Texas culture. For instance, in terms of conservative politics and ideology. In fact, Austin and UT are democratic hot spots (like all major cities in Texas) and in my experience, it seems in many ways just, or even more, as progressive a as Copenhagen and KU.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing the combination of the UT and Texas culture and all of the Americans and international students infused in it all together.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All the research and preperation leadning up to it. During the stay itself, it was probably prioritizing studying vs exploring/socializing.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Do it. Going on exchange at UT has been so extremely enriching and probably one of the best experiences of my life. Even if you don't go to to UT, or Texas or the US, go somewhere. I would say people who don't exploit this opportunity are seriously missing out on so much. It might change your outlook on the the whole world or your own life. See it as a phenomenal investment in yourself.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
